title: 22. Interview: Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS)
summary: Interview Q&A for Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is the HDFS block size 128 MB instead of 4 KB like ext4?
**Answer:** Three reasons: metadata economy, sequential throughput, and seek amortization. (1) **Metadata economy**: the NameNode holds the entire namespace in RAM, with ~150 bytes of metadata per block. A 1 PB file at 4 KB blocks would generate 268 million blocks needing ~40 GB of NameNode RAM — feasible but extreme, and a 100 PB cluster would need 4 TB of RAM. At 128 MB blocks, the same 1 PB file is just 8,192 blocks needing ~1.2 MB of RAM, so a single NameNode can hold petabytes of data. (2) **Sequential throughput**: HDD achieves ~100 MB/s on sequential reads but only ~1 MB/s on random reads because of seek time. A 128 MB block is read as one contiguous chunk, hitting full disk bandwidth. A 4 KB block would be dominated by seek time, making disk throughput collapse. (3) **Seek amortization**: the ~10 ms seek to find a block is amortized across 128 MB of data — seek overhead is 0.008% of read time. At 4 KB, seek would be 80% of read time. The trade-off is poor small-file performance: a 1 KB file still occupies a full 128 MB block on disk and a full metadata entry, so HDFS is explicitly designed for large files. Workloads with many small files (e.g., web crawled HTML) typically concatenate them into SequenceFiles or HAR archives before HDFS storage.
**Visual:**
```
4 KB block:    1 PB file = 268M blocks -> 40 GB NN RAM (unusable)
               random read dominated by 10ms seek (1 MB/s effective)
128 MB block:  1 PB file = 8,192 blocks -> 1.2 MB NN RAM (fine)
               sequential read at 100 MB/s (full HDD bandwidth)
               seek 10ms amortized over 128 MB = 0.008% overhead
trade-off:     1 KB file still uses 128 MB block -> use SequenceFile/HAR
```

### Q2. How does HDFS achieve fault tolerance, and what failure modes does it handle?
**Answer:** HDFS handles four failure modes via replication and re-replication. (1) **DataNode failure** — each DataNode sends a heartbeat to the NameNode every 3 seconds. If the NameNode doesn't receive a heartbeat within 10 minutes (default `dfs.namenode.heartbeat.recheck-interval` = 300s × 2 plus 10s × heartbeat interval), it marks the DataNode as dead. All blocks on that node are marked under-replicated, and the NameNode instructs other DataNodes to copy them to new locations until the replication factor (default 3) is restored — typically within minutes. (2) **Disk failure** — DataNodes report per-disk failures in block reports; the NameNode treats them the same as DataNode failures, re-replicating the affected blocks. JBOD (Just a Bunch Of Disks) is preferred over RAID because RAID-5 rebuilds are slower and more expensive than HDFS's parallel re-replication across many DataNodes. (3) **Rack failure** — replica placement ensures the third replica is on a different rack, so a top-of-rack switch failure or rack power loss leaves 2 replicas intact, preserving data and allowing the cluster to continue serving reads. (4) **NameNode failure** — the active NameNode's state is persisted to disk (EditLog for operations, FsImage for periodic snapshots) on shared storage (NFS or a quorum of JournalNodes). A Standby NameNode (Hadoop 2.x HA) hot-failovers within ~30 seconds using ZooKeeper-based leader election. The combined design tolerates: simultaneous loss of 2 out of 3 replicas (with degraded availability), one entire rack, or one NameNode (with HA) — without data loss.
**Visual:**
```
DataNode failure:  heartbeat missed 10min -> mark dead -> re-replicate blocks
Disk failure:      block report shows disk down -> re-replicate that disk's blocks
Rack failure:      3rd replica on different rack -> 2 replicas survive, cluster continues
NameNode failure:  EditLog + FsImage on shared storage -> Standby NN failover (~30s)
tolerates:         2 of 3 replicas lost (degraded), 1 rack, 1 NameNode (with HA)
JBOD > RAID:       parallel re-replication across nodes is faster than RAID rebuild
```

### Q3. What is rack-awareness and why does replica placement matter?
**Answer:** Rack-awareness is HDFS's knowledge of the physical topology of the cluster — which DataNode is in which rack — and its use of that knowledge to place replicas strategically. The default placement policy for a 3-replica block written by a client on DataNode N in rack R is: replica 1 on N (local, no network), replica 2 on a different node in R (cheap intra-rack write, survives single-node failure), replica 3 on a node in a different rack R' (survives rack failure). The policy balances three concerns: (1) **Write performance** — putting replica 1 local avoids the network for the initial write, replica 2 in-rack uses the higher-bandwidth intra-rack fabric (often 10 Gbps non-blocking), only replica 3 crosses the slower inter-rack link. (2) **Read performance** — reads can be served from any replica, and the client picks the closest (local > intra-rack > inter-rack), so most reads avoid inter-rack traffic. (3) **Fault tolerance** — having one replica on a different rack survives rack-level failures (top-of-rack switch, rack PDU, rack cooling). Without rack-awareness, random placement could put all 3 replicas in the same rack — a single rack failure would lose the data. The trade-off: inter-rack writes consume core switch bandwidth, so high-write clusters may tune the policy (e.g., 2 in-rack, 1 cross-rack is default; some use all-different-rack for ultra-critical data). The NameNode learns topology from a script (`topology.script.file.name`) that maps DataNode IP to rack path like `/datacenter1/rack5`.
**Visual:**
```
3-replica placement (writer on DN1 in rack A):
  replica 1: DN1 (rack A) -- local, no network
  replica 2: DN2 (rack A) -- intra-rack, cheap, survives single-node failure
  replica 3: DN3 (rack B) -- cross-rack, survives rack failure
read:    client picks closest replica -> local > intra-rack > cross-rack
without rack-awareness: 3 random DNs could all be in rack A -> rack failure = data loss
tuning:  critical data -> all different racks; write-heavy -> 2 in-rack + 1 cross
```

### Q4. What is the role of the NameNode, and why is it a single point of failure?
**Answer:** The NameNode is the master of HDFS, holding the entire filesystem namespace (directory tree, file-to-block mapping, block-to-DataNode mapping) in RAM for fast lookups. It handles: (1) metadata operations (create, delete, rename, open file, get block locations); (2) DataNode heartbeat tracking (every 3s) and block report processing (every 6h); (3) replication management (under-replicated blocks trigger re-replication, over-replicated trigger deletion); (4) persistence (EditLog of operations, FsImage snapshots to disk). The NameNode is a single point of failure because all metadata lives in one process's memory — if it crashes without recovery, the entire filesystem is inaccessible (DataNodes still hold block bytes, but no client knows which blocks belong to which file). Pre-Hadoop-2, recovery meant restarting the NameNode from the latest FsImage + replaying the EditLog, which took 10-30 minutes on large clusters — during which the cluster was unavailable. Hadoop 2 introduced **HA (High Availability)**: an Active NameNode and a Standby NameNode, with the Standby hot-tracking the Active's EditLog via a quorum of JournalNodes (3-5 nodes, majority write). On Active failure, ZooKeeper-based failover promotes the Standby in ~30 seconds. The Standby also takes over the EditLog tailing, eliminating the Single Point of Failure. The trade-off: HA requires more hardware (standby NN, JournalNodes, ZooKeeper) and adds operational complexity, so smaller clusters may still run non-HA. The NameNode memory ceiling (typically 400M blocks ≈ 50 PB at 128 MB blocks, 3x replication) is the long-term scaling limit, addressed by HDFS Federation (multiple NameNodes, each owning a slice of the namespace).
**Visual:**
```
NameNode:  namespace tree + file->blocks + block->DNs in RAM
           ~150 bytes/block -> 50 PB cluster needs ~75 GB RAM (at 128 MB blocks)
           heartbeat tracking, block report, replication, persistence
SPOF:      single process -> crash = whole FS unavailable (pre-HA)
HA (2.x):  Active + Standby, EditLog via JournalNode quorum, ZK failover ~30s
Federation: multiple NNs, each owns namespace slice -> scale beyond 1 NN's RAM
```

### Q5. Why does HDFS use a write-once-read-many model, and what does it trade off?
**Answer:** HDFS allows a file to be written once (with optional append added in Hadoop 2.x), then read many times — but never modified in place. This simplifies consistency: there are no distributed locks, no multi-writer coordination, no MVCC, no read-write conflicts. The write pipeline (client -> DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3) is straightforward because only one writer exists per file. Reads always see the file's complete state (no partial writes visible). The trade-off is that HDFS cannot support workloads requiring updates: (1) **Operational databases** — a banking app updating account balances cannot use HDFS as its primary store; it would need to rewrite the entire file on each update, which is absurd. (2) **Random writes** — appending a single record at offset 5,000,000 of a 1 GB file requires rewriting the file from offset 5M onward, which is 200 MB of I/O for a 1 KB update. (3) **Concurrent writers** — multiple processes appending to the same file would require coordination that HDFS deliberately avoids. HDFS excels at: append-only logs (web access logs written by Flume, sensor data), bulk-loaded datasets (Hive fact tables loaded once via `LOAD DATA`), and intermediate computation output (MapReduce/Spark shuffle, model training checkpoints). The model aligns with the batch analytics workload — write the data once via ETL, then read it many times for queries — which is exactly what Hive, Spark, and MapReduce do. For mutable data, HBase (HDFS-backed key-value store) or Kudu (columnar with upserts) sit on top of HDFS and provide mutable access at the cost of more complexity.
**Visual:**
```
WORM:       write once -> read many -> no in-place modify
gains:      no distributed locks, no MVCC, no coordination
            single writer per file -> simple pipeline, atomic close
            reads always see complete state
loses:      random updates (rewrite from offset), concurrent writers,
            operational DB workloads
good for:   append-only logs, bulk-loaded datasets, computation output
            (Hive, MapReduce, Spark)
mutable?:   HBase (KV on HDFS), Kudu (columnar w/ upserts) layer on top
```

### Q6. What is HDFS Federation and when do you need it?
**Answer:** HDFS Federation splits the namespace across multiple independent NameNodes, each owning a slice of the directory tree and the blocks for files under that slice. Pre-Federation, a single NameNode held the entire namespace — bounded by its RAM (typically 50-100 PB at 128 MB blocks, 3x replication, ~400M blocks × 150 bytes = 60 GB RAM). Clusters larger than that ceiling couldn't exist as one HDFS. Federation allows horizontal scaling: the namespace `/user`, `/data`, `/tmp`, `/warehouse` can each be served by a different NameNode, each with its own RAM and its own block pool. DataNodes register with all NameNodes and store blocks from all of them in a single physical pool (block IDs are Nameservice-prefixed to avoid collision). Use cases: (1) **Petabyte+ clusters** — Yahoo, Facebook exceeded 100 PB and needed Federation to scale beyond one NameNode. (2) **Multi-tenant isolation** — different teams' namespaces (e.g., `/marketing`, `/engineering`) can be on different NameNodes, so a runaway job spamming `/marketing` doesn't exhaust the engineering NameNode's RAM. (3) **Performance isolation** — NameNode RPC load is split, so heavy metadata operations (file listings, block reports) on one namespace don't slow others. Trade-offs: (1) cross-namespace operations (a job reading files from two NameNodes) require the client to resolve each path against the right NameNode via `ViewFS` (a virtual namespace); (2) operational complexity increases — more NameNodes to monitor, fail over, and back up; (3) block pool management on DataNodes is more complex. Federation is rarely needed below ~30 PB; most enterprises stay on a single HA NameNode pair. The cloud equivalent — S3 with virtually unlimited namespace — is one reason HDFS adoption has declined.
**Visual:**
```
single NN:    1 NameNode, 1 namespace -> bounded by RAM (~50-100 PB)
              ceiling: 400M blocks x 150B = 60 GB RAM
Federation:   multiple NameNodes, each owns slice:
                NN1 -> /user, /tmp
                NN2 -> /warehouse (analytics)
                NN3 -> /data (ingest)
              DataNodes register with all NNs, store blocks from all (block pool)
need:         petabyte+ clusters, multi-tenant isolation, RPC load split
costs:        ViewFS for cross-namespace paths, more NNs to manage
```

### Q7. Why is HDFS declining in favor of cloud object storage (S3, ADLS, GCS)?
**Answer:** Cloud object storage has replaced HDFS for new deployments since ~2018 for five reasons. (1) **Operational overhead** — running HDFS means managing NameNode HA, DataNode failures, disk replacements, capacity planning, JBOD layouts, and rack topology. S3/ADLS/GCS are fully managed; the cloud provider handles all of this. (2) **Elasticity** — HDFS requires provisioning DataNodes ahead of capacity; if data grows faster than expected, you buy and rack more servers (weeks). S3 is elastic — store 1 GB or 1 PB, no provisioning. (3) **Decoupling storage and compute** — HDFS ties storage to the same cluster that runs compute (MapReduce/Spark), so you pay for compute capacity even when only reading data. S3 lets you spin up a transient Spark cluster, run a query, then tear it down, paying only for the seconds of compute. (4) **Durability** — S3 is 99.999999999% (11 nines) durable by design (cross-region replication built in), vs HDFS's 3x replication (which can lose data during correlated failures). (5) **Cost** — S3 Standard is ~$23/TB-month; an on-prem HDFS cluster including hardware, power, ops staff, and DC space is often $50-100/TB-month at small scale. HDFS retains advantages: (a) **Local disk performance** — Spark reading from local HDFS DataNode disks is 2-5x faster than reading from S3 over the network (no locality), critical for shuffle-heavy or I/O-bound jobs; (b) **No egress fees** — moving data out of S3 to another cloud or on-prem incurs egress charges; (c) **Compliance** — regulated industries (banking, government) may require on-prem data residency. Hybrid: S3 for the data lake, local NVMe/SSD on compute nodes for caching intermediate results (e.g., Spark with Alluxio).
**Visual:**
```
S3 wins:     managed (no NameNode/DataNode ops), elastic (no provisioning),
             decoupled storage+compute (transient clusters), 11-nines durable,
             ~$23/TB-mo (cheaper than on-prem at small scale)
HDFS wins:   local-disk perf (2-5x faster reads), no egress fees,
             compliance data residency, predictable cost at massive scale
hybrid:      S3 data lake + local NVMe cache (Alluxio) on compute nodes
trend:       net-new HDFS rare since 2018; on-prem HDFS maintained but not grown
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your HDFS cluster has 50 million small files (avg 100 KB) and the NameNode is at 80% RAM. What do you do?
**Answer:** This is the classic HDFS small-files problem — 50M files × 150 bytes metadata = 7.5 GB RAM, plus each file's blocks (50M blocks at 1 block each × ~150 bytes = another 7.5 GB), totaling ~15 GB just for these files, plus the rest of the namespace. The fix has three tiers. (1) **Immediate relief — archive small files into larger containers**. Use Hadoop Archive (HAR) to pack many small files into one large `.har` file (still readable via `har://` URL but counts as one file on the NameNode). Or convert to SequenceFile / Parquet: write a MapReduce job that reads all small files in a directory and writes them as key-value pairs (filename → bytes) into a single 1 GB SequenceFile, reducing 10,000 NameNode entries to 8. (2) **Process change — don't write small files in the first place**. If a streaming ingest job (Flume, Kafka Connect) writes one file per minute, change it to roll every 100 MB or 1 hour, whichever comes first. If a MapReduce job writes many small outputs, configure `setNumReduceTasks` to produce fewer, larger output files. (3) **Long-term — federation**. If the small-files workload is intrinsic (e.g., a feature store with millions of model artifacts), split the namespace across multiple NameNodes via Federation, so each NameNode holds a fraction of the files. (4) **Cloud migration** — if feasible, move to S3/ADLS where there is no per-file metadata cost (S3 supports trillions of objects). For now: identify the top 10 directories with the most files, archive them into HAR or SequenceFile, and verify the NameNode RAM drops by 50%+. Add monitoring (HDFS Metrics `FilesTotal` and `BlocksTotal`) with alerts at 70% NameNode RAM so this never recurs silently.
**Visual:**
```
problem:   50M files x 100 KB -> 15 GB NN RAM (just for these files)
immediate: HAR (pack many -> 1 .har file, still readable via har://)
           SequenceFile/Parquet (filename -> bytes, 10k files -> 1 file)
process:   ingest rolls every 100 MB or 1 hr, MR sets numReduceTasks low
long-term: Federation (split namespace across NNs)
           or migrate to S3 (no per-file metadata cost)
monitor:   FilesTotal, BlocksTotal, NN RAM% with alert at 70%
```

### Q2. A DataNode is reporting disk failures on 4 of its 12 disks. What happens, and what should you do?
**Answer:** HDFS is designed to handle disk failures gracefully, but you should still respond promptly. What happens automatically: (1) The DataNode marks the failed disks as bad in its `volumeFailure` metric and stops writing new blocks to them. (2) The DataNode's next block report (every 6 hours, or immediately on `dn restart`) reports the missing blocks to the NameNode. (3) The NameNode marks those blocks under-replicated and triggers re-replication to other DataNodes — typically within minutes, depending on cluster load and replication bandwidth throttling (`dfs.namenode.replication.max-streams`). (4) The DataNode continues serving reads/writes on its remaining 8 disks, so the node itself stays alive (no failover needed). What you should do: (1) **Monitor** — check the DataNode's JMX metrics (`NumFailedVolumes`); alert at >0. (2) **Replace the disks** — physically swap the failed disks; HDFS supports hot-swap (no DataNode restart needed if you run `dfsadmin -reconfig datanode` to reload, or restart the DataNode after replacement). (3) **Verify re-replication completed** — check `dfsadmin -report` for under-replicated blocks; should drop to 0 within an hour. (4) **Investigate root cause** — 4 simultaneous disk failures may indicate a backplane issue, a power supply glitch, or a bad batch of disks (check SMART stats). (5) **Capacity planning** — with 4 disks down, the node's usable capacity dropped by 33%; if the cluster is near full, this may trigger emergency re-replication load. (6) **Don't use RAID** — HDFS already does block replication, and RAID-5 rebuilds are slower than HDFS's parallel re-replication. JBOD is the recommended layout.
**Visual:**
```
auto:       DN marks disks bad -> block report -> NN marks under-repl
            -> re-replicate to other DNs (minutes)
            DN continues on remaining 8 disks (no failover)
ops:        monitor NumFailedVolumes (JMX), alert at >0
            hot-swap disks, dfsadmin -reconfig (no DN restart)
            verify dfsadmin -report: under-repl -> 0 within 1 hr
investigate: 4 simultaneous = backplane? power? bad batch? check SMART
no RAID:    HDFS replication replaces RAID; JBOD preferred
```

### Q3. You need to migrate 2 PB of data from on-prem HDFS to S3. What's the plan?
**Answer:** A phased migration over 4-8 weeks, prioritizing data by access pattern. (1) **Inventory** — use `hdfs dfsadmin -report` and a custom script to list every directory with size, last-modified, and replication factor. Categorize: hot (accessed weekly), warm (monthly), cold (rarely), abandoned (not accessed in 1 year). (2) **Tooling** — use `hadoop distcp` (distributed copy) with the S3A connector for the bulk transfer; it runs as a MapReduce job with many parallel mappers, achieving 5-20 Gbps aggregate throughput on a 10 Gbps WAN. For initial seeding when the WAN is too slow, use AWS Snowball Edge (80 TB per device) or Snowmobile (100 PB) — ship physical devices to AWS. (3) **Phased copy** — copy cold data first (it doesn't change, no consistency concerns), then warm (use distcp's update mode `-update` to sync deltas), then hot (continuous sync via distcp cron or a tool like WANdisco Fusion). (4) **Validation** — after each copy, run a checksum comparison (`hadoop fs -checksum` vs `aws s3api head-object` ETag) on a sample; for Parquet/ORC files, run row count and sum comparisons. (5) **Cut over** — once S3 has all data and continuous sync is current, switch applications from `hdfs://` to `s3a://` URLs. (6) **Decommission HDFS** — put DataNodes in DECOMMISSION state (`hdfs dfsadmin -decommission`), wait for blocks to be replicated off, then physically remove. (7) **Cost optimization** — apply S3 lifecycle policies immediately: cold data to Glacier, abandoned data to expire. (8) **Performance** — S3 is slower than local HDFS for random reads; tune Spark with `--conf spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.experimental.input.fadvise=sequential` for sequential workloads, or use S3 Select for columnar pruning. Watch for the "no locality" issue: S3 reads always go over the network, so provision EC2 with high network bandwidth (10 Gbps+).
**Visual:**
```
inventory:     hdfs dfsadmin -report + custom script
               categorize: hot/warm/cold/abandoned
tooling:       distcp with S3A (parallel mappers, 5-20 Gbps)
               initial seed: Snowball Edge (80 TB) or Snowmobile (100 PB)
phased:        cold first (no change), warm with -update (sync deltas),
               hot with continuous sync (WANdisco Fusion)
validate:      checksum sample, row count + sum on Parquet
cutover:       switch hdfs:// -> s3a:// URLs in applications
decom:         hdfs dfsadmin -decommission -> wait -> physically remove
cost:          immediately apply S3 lifecycle (cold -> Glacier, abandon -> expire)
perf:          S3 no-locality -> high-bandwidth EC2, fadvise=sequential
```

### Q4. A Spark job reading from HDFS is slow — disk I/O is the bottleneck. How do you tune?
**Answer:** Diagnose first, then tune. (1) **Diagnose** — check Spark UI for stage timings; if `Disk I/O` dominates, look at the HDFS DataNode metrics (ganglia/ambari) for disk utilization. Check the input size: if the job reads 1 TB but only uses 3 columns out of 50, the bottleneck is reading unused columns. (2) **File format** — if data is in CSV or JSON, switch to Parquet or ORC (columnar). Spark reads only the columns referenced, dropping 80-95% of I/O. (3) **Compression** — enable Snappy or Zstd compression on Parquet files; reduces I/O 3-5x with ~10% CPU overhead. Snappy is faster, Zstd compresses better. (4) **Partitioning** — partition the data by the most-filtered column (typically `date`); Spark's predicate pushdown skips partitions not matching the filter, e.g., `WHERE date = '2024-03-15'` reads 1 partition instead of 365. (5) **Bucketing** — for joins, bucket both tables on the join key (e.g., `customer_id`); Spark avoids the shuffle since matching buckets are co-located. (6) **Split size** — HDFS reads blocks in parallel; default split is 1 block (128 MB). For skew (a few very large files), reduce `dfs.blocksize` or set `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` to 64 MB to increase parallelism. (7) **Locality** — Spark prefers to run tasks on DataNodes holding the block (`NODE_LOCAL`); if you see many `ANY` locality, increase `spark.locality.wait` (default 3s) to give the scheduler more time to find local slots, or rebalance data with `hdfs balancer`. (8) **Speculative execution** — if one task is slow (bad disk, bad node), enable `spark.speculation=true` to launch a duplicate task and take the first result. (9) **Resource allocation** — increase executor count and cores, but don't oversubscribe disk I/O (1 task per disk is optimal). (10) **Cache hot data** — if the same dataset is read multiple times in the job, `.cache()` it in memory or use Alluxio for cluster-wide caching. Typical tuning: switch CSV to Parquet (10x I/O reduction), partition by date (5-50x for filtered queries), Snappy compression (3x) — combined 50-500x speedup not uncommon.
**Visual:**
```
diagnose:    Spark UI stage timings, HDFS DN disk util, input size vs columns used
format:      CSV/JSON -> Parquet/ORC (columnar, read only needed cols, 10x)
compression: Snappy (fast) or Zstd (better), 3-5x I/O reduction
partition:   by most-filtered col (date) -> predicate pushdown skips partitions
bucket:      on join key -> avoids shuffle for joins
split size:  default 128 MB; reduce for skew (spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes)
locality:    NODE_LOCAL > RACK_LOCAL > ANY; spark.locality.wait=3s default
speculation: spark.speculation=true for slow-task mitigation
cache:       .cache() for repeated reads; Alluxio for cluster-wide cache
```

### Q5. Your NameNode takes 45 minutes to restart. How do you reduce this?
**Answer:** A 45-minute NameNode restart means it's loading the FsImage (a snapshot of the namespace) and replaying the EditLog (operations since the last snapshot) — for a large, active cluster, both can be huge. Fixes in priority order: (1) **Enable HA** — a Standby NameNode hot-failovers in ~30 seconds, eliminating restart pain for planned and unplanned outages. This is the single most impactful change. (2) **Checkpoint more frequently** — the Secondary NameNode (or the Standby in HA) merges EditLog into FsImage periodically; default is every hour (`dfs.namenode.checkpoint.period=3600`) or 1 million transactions. Reduce to every 15 minutes or 100K transactions so the EditLog never grows large enough to slow restart. (3) **Tune FsImage loading** — the NameNode loads FsImage serially; Hadoop 3 added parallel loading (`dfs.image.parallel.load=true`) which uses multiple threads, cutting load time 2-4x on multi-core NameNodes. (4) **Reduce namespace size** — if the cluster has 100M+ small files, address the small-files problem (HAR, SequenceFile, Federation) so the FsImage is smaller. (5) **Memory-map the FsImage** — Hadoop 3.2+ supports memory-mapped FsImage loading which is faster than stream parsing; ensure `dfs.image.memory-mapped` is enabled. (6) **Persistent memory for EditLog** — using Intel Optane or NVMe for the EditLog directory reduces write latency dramatically, allowing more operations per second before the EditLog grows. (7) **Avoid huge EditLog transactions** — some operations (e.g., `concat` of many files) generate large EditLog entries; minimize them. After HA + frequent checkpointing + parallel loading, restarts drop from 45 min to under 5 min, and with HA the question becomes moot (no client-visible downtime).
**Visual:**
```
slow restart:  load FsImage (snapshot) + replay EditLog (ops since snapshot)
               both can be huge on large active cluster
fix 1 (best):  enable HA -> Standby hot-failover ~30s, no restart pain
fix 2:         checkpoint more often: every 15 min or 100K transactions
               (default: 1 hour / 1M transactions -> EditLog grows large)
fix 3:         Hadoop 3 parallel FsImage loading (dfs.image.parallel.load=true)
               2-4x speedup on multi-core NN
fix 4:         address small-files problem -> smaller FsImage
fix 5:         memory-mapped FsImage (Hadoop 3.2+, dfs.image.memory-mapped)
fix 6:         NVMe or Optane for EditLog directory (lower write latency)
result:        45 min -> <5 min, or 0 client downtime with HA
```

### Q6. You're designing an HDFS cluster for a 5 PB data lake with mixed workloads. What's the hardware spec?
**Answer:** Hardware sizing for 5 PB usable, 3x replication = 15 PB raw. Cluster design: (1) **NameNode** — 1 active + 1 standby (HA), each with 256 GB RAM (15 PB / 128 MB × 3 replicas × 150B = ~55 GB metadata, plus headroom), 16-core CPU, NVMe SSDs for EditLog (2x1 TB RAID-1). Add 3 JournalNodes (small boxes, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD) for HA consensus, and 3-5 ZooKeeper nodes for leader election. (2) **DataNodes** — 50-100 nodes, each with 12-24 × 8-16 TB HDD (150-400 TB raw per node), JBOD (no RAID), 256 GB RAM (for DataNode + Spark/YARN NodeManager + cache), 2 × 10 Gbps NIC (bonded), dual power supplies. At 200 TB per node, 75 DataNodes provide 15 PB raw. (3) **Rack layout** — 5-10 racks of 8-15 DataNodes each, each rack with 2 top-of-rack switches (redundant) and 40 Gbps uplinks to the spine. Rack-awareness is critical: the default 3-replica policy needs at least 2 racks for the third replica. (4) **Network** — non-blocking 10 Gbps to each DataNode, 40-100 Gbps spine; Spark shuffles generate huge east-west traffic, so oversubscription <2:1 is ideal. (5) **Compute** — YARN NodeManagers on every DataNode (compute and storage co-located for locality); allocate ~50% of RAM to YARN containers, ~25% to OS/caches, ~25% reserved. Spark executors typically 4-8 cores, 16-32 GB each. (6) **Power & cooling** — 15 PB × 4 W/TB (HDD) + overhead = ~60 kW for storage, plus ~40 kW for compute = 100 kW total; one DC cage with N+1 power and cooling. (7) **Software** — Hadoop 3.x, kerberos for security, Ranger for ACLs, Oozie or Airflow for scheduling, Ambari or Cloudera Manager for ops. Cost: ~$3-5M hardware + $0.5-1M/year ops. Consider cloud alternative: S3 + EMR for ~$100K/month, no upfront capex — usually cheaper below 3-year horizon.

### Q7. How would you secure an HDFS cluster handling sensitive financial data?
**Answer:** Defense in depth across authentication, authorization, encryption, and audit. (1) **Authentication — Kerberos**. HDFS trusts whatever user the OS reports by default; in a multi-tenant cluster this is unacceptable. Enable Kerberos (`hadoop.security.authentication=kerberos`); every HDFS RPC must present a Kerberos ticket, so users and services (Hive, Spark) authenticate against the corporate AD/KDC. Keytabs (long-lived Kerberos credentials) for services; users get tickets via `kinit`. (2) **Authorization — Ranger or Sentry**. HDFS file permissions (POSIX-style `rwx` with owner/group) are too coarse for sensitive data. Install Apache Ranger for fine-grained ACLs at the file/column level, with policies like "Risk team can read `sensitive/transactions.cc_number` masked, but Ops can only see `sensitive/transactions.amount`". Ranger integrates with Kerberos so the identity is trusted. (3) **Encryption at rest — HDFS Transparent Encryption**. Create encryption zones (per-directory) with a Hadoop Key Management Server (KMS) backed by a hardware HSM or KeyTrustee. Files in `/sensitive` are encrypted with zone keys; data on disk and in backups is unreadable without the KMS. (4) **Encryption in transit — TLS**. All HDFS RPC and HTTP traffic over Wire Encryption (`hadoop.rpc.protection=privacy`), and HTTPS for WebHDFS. (5) **Data masking** — Ranger masking policies mask or hash PII columns (SSN, account numbers) for non-privileged users; only the Risk team sees raw values. (6) **Audit — Ranger Audit to SIEM**. Every file access, ACL change, and KMS key use is logged and shipped to Splunk/ELK for monitoring and compliance reports (SOX, PCI-DSS). (7) **Network isolation** — HDFS cluster on a private VLAN, accessible only via a bastion host; DataNodes don't have public IPs. (8) **Patch management** — quarterly Hadoop security patches, monthly OS patches. (9) **Secure ingest** — Flume/Kafka with Kerberos and TLS; no plaintext data over the wire. (10) **Backup encryption** — HDFS snapshots to another cluster or to S3 must also be encrypted (Snapshot DistCp with `-p` preserves encryption). The full stack is heavy operational lift; for regulated financial data, it's mandatory, but many organizations choose to keep such data in a separate, locked-down cluster rather than the multi-tenant data lake.
**Visual:**
```
authn:      Kerberos on all RPCs (users kinit, services use keytabs)
authz:      Apache Ranger for fine-grained ACLs (file + column level)
            policy: Risk team reads cc_number masked, Ops sees amount only
encrypt rest: HDFS Transparent Encryption zones, KMS backed by HSM
encrypt transit: Wire Encryption (rpc.protection=privacy), HTTPS for WebHDFS
masking:    Ranger masking policies hash PII for non-privileged users
audit:      Ranger Audit -> Splunk/ELK for SOX/PCI compliance reports
network:    private VLAN, bastion host, DataNodes no public IP
patch:      quarterly Hadoop security patches, monthly OS patches
ingest:     Flume/Kafka with Kerberos + TLS (no plaintext)
backup:     Snapshot DistCp -p preserves encryption to DR cluster/S3
ops lift:   heavy; consider separate locked-down cluster for sensitive data
```

quiz.explanation: Three reasons: metadata economy, sequential throughput, and seek amortization. (1) Metadata economy: the NameNode holds the entire namespace in RAM, with ~150 bytes of metadata per block. A 1 PB file at 4 KB blocks would generate 268 million blocks needing ~40 GB of NameNode RAM — feasible but extreme, and a 100 PB cluster would need 4 TB of RAM.

quiz.explanation: HDFS allows a file to be written once (with optional append added in Hadoop 2.x), then read many times — but never modified in place. This simplifies consistency: there are no distributed locks, no multi-writer coordination, no MVCC, no read-write conflicts. The write pipeline (client -> DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3) is straightforward because only one writer exists per file.
